questions.stem: State what happens to the pressure of a fixed gas at constant temperature when its volume is halved.
questions.modelAnswer: The pressure rises — in the ideal case it doubles — because the same molecules collide with the walls more frequently in the smaller volume.

questions.stem: State the two conditions that must hold when relating pressure and volume of a fixed gas.
questions.modelAnswer: The temperature must be constant and the amount of gas must be fixed.

questions.stem: Explain, using the kinetic model, why the pressure of a gas falls as it is slowly expanded at constant temperature.
questions.modelAnswer: The molecules keep the same average speeds because the temperature is unchanged, so each collision delivers the same impulse. But in the larger volume each molecule travels further between wall impacts, so each wall receives fewer collisions per second. The total impulse per unit area per second — the pressure — therefore falls.

questions.stem: A vacuum pump removes air from around a sealed balloon, which swells to twice its size. Sketch the reasoning linking the change in available volume to the change in the trapped gas's pressure.
questions.modelAnswer: As the outside squeeze falls, the trapped gas expands into a larger volume at the same temperature. With longer flight paths between wall hits, the internal collision rate per unit area falls, so the internal pressure drops until it balances the reduced outside pressure — the pressure falls as the volume grows.

questions.stem: State what happens to the pressure of a fixed gas at constant volume when its kelvin temperature is increased.
questions.modelAnswer: The pressure increases in step with the kelvin temperature, because faster molecules strike the walls harder and more often.

questions.stem: State the two ways in which faster molecules intensify the wall bombardment.
questions.modelAnswer: Each collision delivers a larger impulse, and the molecules return to the walls sooner so collisions happen more frequently.

questions.stem: Explain why the pressure–temperature relationship requires the amount of gas to be fixed.
questions.modelAnswer: Pressure is produced by the total bombardment of all the molecules present. Adding or removing molecules changes the number of impactors independently of temperature, so the clean correspondence between kelvin temperature and pressure would be broken. Fixing the amount of gas isolates temperature as the only driver of the collision totals.

questions.stem: A rigid gas cylinder left in direct sun warms from 300 K to 330 K. Using the qualitative proportionality, state roughly how the internal pressure changes.
questions.modelAnswer: At fixed volume pressure tracks kelvin temperature, so the pressure rises by about a tenth — roughly 10% higher — because 330 K is 10% above 300 K.
